strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-served problem: unsupervised model selection and misspecification diagnosis for Bayesian imaging inverse problems when only noisy partial measurements are available and no ground truth exists.

The core idea of combining data fission with Bayesian cross-validation is conceptually elegant and well matched to imaging settings. The Gaussian and Poisson constructions are plausible, and the connection to posterior predictive checks and marginal likelihoods helps clarify what the method is estimating.

The methodology is broadly compatible with modern posterior samplers, including plug-and-play Langevin and diffusion-based samplers, which makes the contribution potentially useful beyond a narrow model class.

The experiments cover several relevant scenarios: likelihood/kernel selection, natural-image prior OOD detection, Poisson noise, and MRI reconstruction. The reported results are consistently stronger than the residual-based baselines in the kernel-selection experiment and show good detection power in several OOD settings.

The appendix gives useful implementation details and additional diagnostics, including sensitivity to alpha, Monte Carlo error in the Gaussian case, Poisson data fission, and MRI failure cases. The paper is generally well written and the limitations of the perceptual posterior score are at least partly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is still somewhat limited for the strength of the claims. The kernel-selection experiment uses only three images and 15 single-shot cases; the natural-image and MRI studies use modest test sizes and relatively controlled ID/OOD splits. This makes the reported high accuracies less convincing as evidence of broad reliability.

There is little formal theory beyond the data-fission construction and Gaussian sanity checks. In particular, the paper does not provide guarantees that the proposed scores consistently rank models under realistic misspecification, finite alpha, finite Monte Carlo sampling, or learned/improper priors.

The posterior-based score is heuristic and embedding-dependent. The MRI appendix explicitly shows cases where LPIPS favors the wrong prior because it is not appropriate for medical images, and the main method gives no principled guidance for choosing or validating embeddings in a new domain.

The claim of operating from a single measurement needs more nuance. Model comparison can be single-measurement, but the OOD testing procedure calibrates thresholds using a reference ID dataset, so the formal test is not purely based on one measurement alone.

Computational cost is not characterized rigorously. The method is presented as low cost, but experiments still require many posterior samples or diffusion/PIDAL iterations, and there are no wall-clock comparisons, scaling studies, or resource-normalized comparisons against stronger alternatives.

Baseline coverage is thin. Kernel selection is compared mainly to residual-based methods, while the OOD experiments do not compare against recent diffusion OOD methods except by discussion, despite related work being cited.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as provided: the reproducibility section contains blank code/model links, and important hyperparameters such as alpha, embedding choice, sampler settings, and thresholds appear tuned per setting. This may be an anonymization artifact, but reviewers cannot verify the release from the paper text.

The paper lacks a substantive ethics or risk discussion. This is especially relevant because the method is demonstrated on MRI reconstruction and hallucination-prone diffusion priors; false reassurance from a misspecification test could have downstream clinical consequences.

Presentation is mostly clear, but there are some notation and proofreading issues, including malformed equations/brackets, duplicated references, and occasional ambiguity about whether higher or lower score is preferred for each estimator.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and important problem in Bayesian computational imaging: unsupervised model selection and misspecification detection when only a single noisy measurement is available and ground truth is absent. This is a meaningful setting for inverse problems with modern learned priors.

The proposed combination of data fission with Bayesian cross-validation is conceptually appealing. The split-measurement construction gives a plausible way to create held-out predictive checks from one observation, and the connection to posterior predictive checks and marginal likelihood in limiting cases helps position the method.

The paper covers several relevant experimental settings, including likelihood/kernel selection, natural-image prior/OOD detection with diffusion priors, Poisson noise, and MRI reconstruction. These examples suggest the method can be integrated with plug-and-play Langevin and diffusion-based posterior samplers.

The manuscript is generally well organized, and the appendix provides useful implementation details and additional results, including sensitivity to the split parameter alpha and examples of failure cases. The limitations of estimator convergence, alpha choice, and embedding dependence are at least partly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The central claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The method is presented as a general framework for Bayesian model selection and misspecification testing, but the paper provides limited theoretical guarantees beyond known data-fission identities and standard Monte Carlo reasoning. There is no rigorous characterization of when the proposed scores reliably select the correct model or detect misspecification in high-dimensional inverse problems.

The empirical evaluation is too narrow and small for the breadth of the claims. The kernel-selection experiment uses only three images and five closely specified kernels; the OOD experiments use modest dataset sizes and highly separated domains in several cases, such as faces versus dogs/bedrooms or brain versus knee MRI. These settings do not convincingly establish robustness in harder, more realistic model-selection regimes.

The baselines are insufficient. For likelihood selection, the comparison is mainly to residual-based Bayesian methods; for OOD/prior misspecification, there is little direct comparison to recent diffusion OOD methods, posterior predictive checks, supervised/unsupervised distribution-shift detectors, marginal-likelihood approximations where feasible, or simpler reconstruction-quality and sample-variance heuristics. This makes it difficult to attribute the reported performance to the proposed Bayesian cross-validation principle rather than to task-specific score choices.

The posterior-based score depends heavily on the embedding or perceptual metric, but this dependence is not resolved. The paper notes that LPIPS can be inappropriate for MRI and that DINOv2 improves some results, which undercuts the claim of an objective general diagnostic unless the embedding-selection problem is addressed more systematically.

The method appears computationally expensive despite being described as low cost. The procedure requires repeated posterior sampling for multiple noise splits, and the appendix shows slow Monte Carlo convergence in the Gaussian analysis. The paper argues that exact convergence is unnecessary for ranking, but this is supported empirically rather than theoretically and may fail in close model comparisons.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript. Some details are provided in the appendix, but the main text contains placeholder or missing code/model links after 'available at', and important choices such as thresholds, alpha, number of noise splits, posterior-sampler settings, embeddings, and prior calibration are task-specific and likely sensitive.

The paper does not sufficiently discuss ethical and practical risks for scientific or medical imaging. In MRI examples, the method is used to diagnose prior mismatch, but hallucinated anatomical structure and incorrect acceptance of a misspecified prior could have serious downstream implications. The paper would benefit from clearer guidance that this is a diagnostic aid rather than a validation guarantee.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: evaluating Bayesian imaging models and diagnosing misspecification without ground-truth images, especially for modern implicit priors such as diffusion and plug-and-play samplers.

The core idea of combining Bayesian cross-validation with data fission is elegant and well motivated. The connection to posterior predictive checks and to marginal likelihood in the alpha -> 0 limit helps clarify what the proposed criterion is estimating.

The methodology is broadly applicable across likelihoods and samplers. The paper demonstrates Gaussian and Poisson settings, plug-and-play Langevin sampling, diffusion posterior sampling, natural image deblurring, and MRI reconstruction.

The empirical results are convincing enough for the main claims: likelihood-model selection substantially outperforms residual baselines in the blur-kernel experiment, and the posterior/perceptual score gives strong OOD detection performance in natural images and MRI.

The presentation is generally clear, with useful intuition about the role of alpha, the distinction between likelihood-based and posterior-based scores, and why held-out synthetic measurements can expose prior misspecification.

The supplement adds meaningful implementation detail and diagnostic experiments, including convergence behavior, kernel-selection tables, Poisson noise experiments, and model-selection results for MRI.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are limited. Data fission gives conditional independence under the assumed noise model, but the paper does not provide formal consistency, calibration, or error bounds for the proposed model-selection or OOD-testing procedures beyond the Gaussian toy analysis.

The posterior-based score is heuristic and depends strongly on the embedding/discrepancy choice. The MRI supplement notes that LPIPS can be inappropriate for medical images and that DINOv2 changes accuracy substantially, which weakens the general claim unless embedding selection is better principled.

The OOD detection experiments require an in-distribution reference set to set the 95th-percentile threshold. This is reasonable, but it should be stated more prominently because it qualifies the “single measurement” and “fully unsupervised” framing for misspecification testing.

The empirical scope is strong but still somewhat small in places: the blur-kernel selection uses only three test images, and some reported accuracies are over small datasets without confidence intervals or repeated random seeds.

Computational cost is described as low, but the method still requires repeated posterior sampling under several data splits and models. A clearer wall-clock/runtime comparison to baselines and to standard posterior sampling would make the efficiency claim more convincing.

Some implementation and reproducibility details appear incomplete in the manuscript text, with blank code/model download locations in the reproducibility section. The supplement gives many details, but acceptance-quality reproducibility depends on these links and exact scripts being available.

There are minor notation and presentation issues, for example the data-fission definitions contain apparent sign/function-label typos, and the discussion of which scores are proper versus heuristic could be sharper.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and under-addressed problem: unsupervised model selection and misspecification diagnosis for Bayesian imaging inverse problems when ground truth and repeated measurements are unavailable.

The core idea of combining Bayesian cross-validation with data fission/noise splitting is elegant and well matched to imaging settings. The connection to posterior predictive checks and the limiting relation to marginal likelihood as alpha goes to zero provide useful statistical intuition.

The methodology is broadly compatible with modern posterior samplers, including plug-and-play Langevin and diffusion posterior samplers, and the paper demonstrates this across Gaussian deblurring, diffusion priors, Poisson noise, and MRI reconstruction.

The experiments are thoughtfully organized: likelihood misspecification is tested via blur-kernel selection; prior misspecification is tested with natural-image and MRI OOD examples; appendices include ablations for alpha, embeddings, sample degradation, and computational cost.

The empirical results are promising: the blur-kernel experiment reports 86.7% single-shot and 100% few-shot accuracy versus substantially weaker residual baselines; OOD detection achieves near-target type-I error and high power for strong OOD cases; MRI brain/knee experiments show strong separation.
The paper is generally well written and gives substantial implementation detail in the appendix, including pseudocode, sampler settings, runtime estimates, and additional numerical tables.
weaknesses: The central claims are somewhat broader than the evidence. The experiments are convincing as demonstrations, but still limited: the blur-kernel selection uses only three images and five hand-designed kernels, and several OOD evaluations rely on relatively small curated subsets with clear distribution shifts.

The OOD testing setup is not fully 'single-measurement' in practice because the threshold is calibrated from a reference in-distribution dataset. This is reasonable, but it should be stated more carefully since it weakens the strongest unsupervised/single-observation framing.

Theoretical support is partial. The marginal-likelihood connection is shown only for a specific likelihood-style score and in an alpha-to-zero limit that is computationally challenging; the posterior/perceptual score used for prior misspecification is more heuristic and depends strongly on the chosen embedding.

The method has nontrivial computational cost despite being cheaper than nested sampling. The reported DiffPIR setup takes about 1802 seconds per image on a V100 for the natural-image experiment, which makes the 'low computational cost' claim relative rather than absolute.

Sensitivity to hyperparameters and design choices remains material. Performance depends on alpha, the number of fissions/samples, sampler quality, and the embedding used in Phi2; the appendix shows CLIP performs poorly and DreamSim can increase type-I error.

Baselines are limited for prior/OOD experiments. The paper compares likelihood selection to residual methods and includes a ProxNest sanity check on a denoising example, but does not extensively compare OOD detection against recent unsupervised or sampler-based alternatives under matched assumptions.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing or blank code/data links in the manuscript's Software and Data section. Although many implementation details are provided, the actual release information appears absent in the submitted PDF.

The impact/ethics statement is boilerplate and does not discuss risks specific to scientific or medical imaging, such as false reassurance from model diagnostics, hallucinated structures, or downstream clinical/scientific decisions.

There are some presentation issues and notation slips, e.g. equation (3) appears to label both split variables with f^- rather than f^+ and f^-, and some extracted text suggests minor formatting/citation glitches. These do not undermine the main idea but should be cleaned up.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: unsupervised model selection and misspecification diagnosis for Bayesian imaging inverse problems when ground truth is unavailable.

The central idea of combining data fission with Bayesian cross-validation is natural and potentially useful, especially because it can be wrapped around existing posterior samplers rather than requiring model-specific marginal likelihood machinery.

The manuscript gives a reasonably clear high-level presentation, includes pseudo-code, discusses computational cost, and provides experiments across Gaussian toy models, deblurring, Poisson noise, and MRI reconstruction.

The comparison to proximal nested sampling in the appendix is a useful sanity check: the proposed scores rank simple denoising priors consistently with estimated evidence and supervised PSNR in that setting.
weaknesses: The evidence does not support the breadth of the claims. The main likelihood-selection experiment uses only three images and five synthetic blur kernels, with 15 single-shot cases total; reporting 86.7% or 100% accuracy from such a small setup is not convincing for a general model-selection method.

The OOD experiments are also limited and partly easy: strong OOD categories such as bedrooms, natural images, dogs, and knee scans versus brain scans create large visual/domain gaps. The harder moderate-OOD cases degrade substantially under blur, but the paper still frames the method as broadly excellent.

The paper provides little theory for the actual scoring rules used in the experiments. The marginal-likelihood connection is shown only for a particular likelihood-based choice and an alpha -> 0 limit, while the practical LPIPS/posterior discrepancy score is heuristic and not shown to be proper, calibrated, or consistent for model selection or hypothesis testing.

The statistical testing procedure is underdeveloped. Thresholds are set from small reference sets, but there are no confidence intervals, uncertainty estimates, correction for multiple settings/embeddings, or analysis of how many reference samples are needed to control Type I error reliably.

Important baselines are missing. For OOD detection, the paper mostly demonstrates separability rather than comparing against established unsupervised OOD or posterior predictive approaches under the same inverse-problem setting. For model selection, the main baseline comparison is narrow and weak.

The method is computationally expensive despite being presented as low-cost: the appendix reports about 1802 seconds per image for DiffPIR with the chosen setup on a V100. This may still be cheaper than nested sampling, but it is not clearly practical for routine model diagnosis.

There are presentation and reproducibility problems. The software/data section has empty placeholders for code and data links, and several implementation details are scattered in the appendix. Some notation/sign conventions are confusing, e.g. log-likelihood versus squared-error objectives and whether scores are minimized or maximized.

Limitations and ethics are treated superficially. The impact statement is boilerplate, and the paper does not seriously discuss risks of using these diagnostics in high-stakes scientific or medical imaging when a misspecified but visually plausible prior may pass the proposed checks.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: selecting and diagnosing Bayesian imaging models from noisy partial measurements without ground truth. This is highly relevant for modern learned priors in inverse problems, especially in scientific and medical imaging where supervised validation is often unavailable.

The central idea of combining Bayesian cross-validation with data fission is elegant and well motivated. It gives a clear operational procedure for turning a single measurement into paired pseudo-measurements and evaluating predictive consistency.

The method is sampler-agnostic and therefore broadly applicable to plug-and-play Langevin samplers, diffusion posterior samplers, and other Bayesian imaging pipelines. This makes the contribution more useful than a method tied to one prior architecture.

The paper provides useful theoretical context, including the relation to posterior predictive checking and a limiting connection to marginal likelihood as the splitting parameter tends to zero. The Gaussian analysis helps clarify the role of the splitting parameter and the computational tradeoff.

The empirical section is broad and convincing overall: likelihood/kernel selection, natural-image prior misspecification, MRI reconstruction, Poisson noise, embedding ablations, comparison to proximal nested sampling, and runtime discussion. The reported results are consistently strong, including 86.7% single-shot and 100% few-shot kernel selection, high OOD power for natural images, and strong MRI OOD detection.
Presentation is generally clear. The paper explains why standard marginal-likelihood and posterior-predictive approaches are difficult in imaging, and the algorithmic recipe is easy to follow.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are still limited relative to the breadth of the claims. The marginal-likelihood limit is shown for a particular scoring choice and under restrictive bounded-continuity assumptions, while the main practical estimators, especially the posterior/embedding-based score, remain largely heuristic.

The posterior-based score depends strongly on the chosen embedding and splitting parameter. The ablations are useful, but they also show meaningful sensitivity: CLIP performs poorly, DreamSim can inflate type-I error, and performance for moderate OOD cases drops with stronger blur. More guidance or theory for choosing alpha and embeddings would strengthen the method.

Some experiments use small or specialized evaluation sets. The likelihood selection experiment is based on only three images and synthetic blur kernels; the OOD experiments, while broader, still rely on controlled degradations and relatively small reference/test sets. This limits confidence about robustness in less curated real deployments.

The OOD testing procedure requires a reference in-distribution set to set the 95th-percentile threshold. This is reasonable, but it weakens the paper's strongest framing around diagnosis from a single measurement and should be made more explicit.

Baseline coverage is somewhat uneven. The likelihood selection comparison includes Bayesian residual methods and a nested-sampling comparison appears in the appendix, but the OOD experiments would benefit from stronger or more directly comparable unsupervised OOD baselines for inverse problems where possible.

Reproducibility is not fully satisfactory in the manuscript as provided: the Software and Data section states that code, models, and images are available, but the actual links are blank in the PDF. The appendix gives many implementation details, which helps, but executable code and exact data splits are important for a method with many sampler, embedding, and threshold choices.

The limitations and ethics discussion are thin. The impact statement is generic, and the paper should more directly discuss failure modes in high-stakes scientific/medical imaging, especially since the method may be used to decide whether a learned prior is trustworthy.
